item.title: From Outbreak Size to Transmissibility: Imperial’s Third COVID-19 Report
item.dc:creator: Jong-Hoon Kim
item.description:
A new question: could the outbreak sustain itself?

In the previous post, we saw how a few cases detected abroad revealed a much larger outbreak in Wuhan. Imperial College London’s first two reports used travel data and overseas detections to estimate its size. Report 2 estimated 4,000 cases with symptom onset by 18 January 2020, with an uncertainty range of 1,000–9,700. (1)

The third report, published on 25 January 2020, used those estimates to ask whether human-to-human transmission could sustain the outbreak. Imperial’s report summary

The central quantity was the basic reproduction number, : the average number of new infections caused by one infected person in a fully susceptible population before control measures. Under stable conditions, chains shrink on average when and can grow when . Individual chains can still die out by chance. (2)

We will read the report in its January 2020 setting, distinguish evidence from assumptions, and reconstruct its simulation in R. We will compare the results with Figure 1 and Table 1, examine the intervals’ statistical meaning, and contrast the approach with Riou and Althaus’s Bayesian analysis, published five days later.

What Imperial knew—and what it assumed

The analysis combined an inferred outbreak size with assumptions about transmission. (1,3)

Input Report’s starting point Evidential status
Outbreak size 4,000 cases by 18 January; alternatives of 1,000 and 9,700 Previous estimate from exported cases
Initial animal-to-human cases Scenarios spanning 40–200 Unknown quantity explored through assumptions
Generation time Baseline mean of 8.4 days Borrowed from SARS
Individual transmission Substantial variation, following SARS Assumed for the new virus

The inferred case total was uncertain because travel, detection and reporting were imperfect. Using its point estimate as a fixed input leaves that uncertainty unaccounted for.

The total also combines initial animal-to-human infections with subsequent human-to-human infections. Outbreak size alone cannot separate them; the assumed number of initial cases determines how much onward transmission the model must explain.

How the report turned a case count into a reproduction number

Figure 1 shows 5,000 simulated epidemics starting from 40 animal-to-human infections in December 2019, with SARS-like generation time and variation in infectiousness. The red curve is the median cumulative count; the grey band is the central 95% range. Light grey lines show individual trajectories, and dotted lines mark 18 January and 4,000 cases. (3)

For each candidate , the report recorded the proportion of simulations reaching at least 4,000 cases by 18 January and defined three estimates. (3)

  • Best case (most optimistic): the at which 5% reach the target. Smaller values rarely produce an outbreak this large.
  • Central estimate: the at which 50% reach the target. At this value, the median in Figure 1 passes through the dotted lines’ intersection.
  • Worst case (most pessimistic): the at which 95% reach the target. Larger values usually exceed it.

Repeating this rule across seed counts from 40 to 200 and alternative outbreak sizes produced Table 1. Although the report did not describe it in statistical terms, the rule can be understood as test inversion: its best and worst cases form an approximately 90% confidence interval under fixed assumptions. We will examine that interpretation below.

A stochastic model represents possible histories

Five infected people might cause 0, 0, 1, 1 and 8 subsequent infections—an average of two, with substantial individual variation. A stochastic model represents the different outbreak histories this variation can produce. Even with a known , histories would differ; observing one history leaves uncertainty about the that generated it.

Imperial compared these possible histories with the inferred outbreak size. Fitting a growth curve through the first two reports’ totals would have been unreliable: Report 2 warned that sparse observations, reporting delays and incomplete onset information prevented a dependable growth-rate estimate. (1,3)

Building the model in R

Reconstructing the model requires several choices the report left unstated.

Ingredient Stated in Report 3 Used here
Zoonotic (seed) cases 40 in the baseline; 80 to 200 also explored 40 and 200
Timing of the seed cases “December 2019” A single day, calibrated below
Offspring distribution Negative binomial with , as estimated for SARS Same
Generation time Mean 8.4 days, as estimated for SARS Gamma distribution, mean 8.4 and SD 3.8 days

Number of simulations 5,000 5,000 for the figure; 2,000 per value for estimation
Depletion of susceptibles Not mentioned None; a pure branching process

Lipsitch and colleagues’ SARS analysis supplied the generation-time mean and standard deviation; Report 3 cited only the mean. (4) Lloyd-Smith and colleagues supplied the SARS dispersion estimate, . (2) A few thousand infections would barely deplete Wuhan’s susceptible population of roughly eleven million.

A branching process with superspreading

Following the SARS literature, the report models each person’s number of secondary infections, , as negative binomial with mean and dispersion :

Small produces large variance: most people infect nobody, while a few infect many. (2) Secondary infections occur after gamma-distributed generation intervals with the SARS mean and standard deviation. Starting with 40 seed infections, the process continues through the observation window.

Two probabilities describe the process: , the chance of infecting nobody, and , the chance that a single case’s chain eventually dies out. The latter is the smallest solution of

where the right-hand side is the probability generating function of evaluated at . (2) I discussed this extinction probability in a previous post.

Show code 
target_date  <- as.Date("2020-01-18")  # date of Report 2's outbreak-size estimate
target_cases <- 4000                    # Report 2's central estimate
report_date  <- as.Date("2020-01-25")  # Report 3's publication date; end of plot

R0_baseline <- 2.6    # Report 3's central estimate for 40 zoonotic cases
k_sars      <- 0.16   # offspring dispersion estimated for SARS
gt_mean     <- 8.4    # SARS generation time, mean in days
gt_sd       <- 3.8    # SARS generation time, SD in days

# Gamma distribution with the stated mean and SD
gt_shape <- (gt_mean / gt_sd)^2
gt_rate  <- gt_mean / gt_sd^2
Show code 
p_zero <- dnbinom(0, size = k_sars, mu = R0_baseline)

offspring_pgf <- function(s, R0, k) (1 + R0 * (1 - s) / k)^(-k)
extinction_prob <- uniroot(function(q) offspring_pgf(q, R0_baseline, k_sars) - q,
                           interval = c(0, 1 - 1e-9), tol = 1e-10)$root

round(c(proportion_infecting_nobody        = p_zero,
        single_chain_extinction_prob  = extinction_prob,
        expected_surviving_chains_of_40 = 40 * (1 - extinction_prob)), 3)
    proportion_infecting_nobody    single_chain_extinction_prob 
                          0.634                           0.787 
expected_surviving_chains_of_40 
                          8.505

At and , about 63% of people infect nobody, and a single-case chain dies out with probability 0.79. Only about 9 of the 40 seeds are expected to start persistent chains. Their survival and the timing of large clusters drive the variation shown in Figure 1’s grey band.

The simulator

For each generation, the simulator draws offspring counts and infection times, discards infections beyond the observation window, and tallies the rest by day. Descendants always occur after their parents, so discarding late infections cannot remove an earlier descendant.

Show code 
simulate_outbreak <- function(R0, k, n_seed, n_days,
                              max_cases = Inf,
                              gt_shape, gt_rate) {
  # Cumulative infections at the end of each day 0, 1, ..., n_days - 1.
  # Day 0 is the day on which all n_seed zoonotic infections occur.
  # Stops early once max_cases infections have accumulated (for threshold checks).
  daily <- numeric(n_days)
  daily[1] <- n_seed
  n_total <- n_seed
  infection_times <- rep(0, n_seed)

  while (length(infection_times) > 0 && n_total < max_cases) {
    offspring <- rnbinom(length(infection_times), size = k, mu = R0)
    n_offspring <- sum(offspring)
    if (n_offspring == 0) break
    new_times <- rep(infection_times, times = offspring) +
      rgamma(n_offspring, shape = gt_shape, rate = gt_rate)
    new_times <- new_times[new_times < n_days]   # outside the window: ignore
    if (length(new_times) == 0) break
    daily <- daily + tabulate(floor(new_times) + 1, nbins = n_days)
    n_total <- n_total + length(new_times)
    infection_times <- new_times
  }
  cumsum(daily)
}

Most later calculations need only the final size. The helper stops each simulation once it reaches a cap: smaller sizes are exact, while larger values mean “at least the cap” and suffice for threshold comparisons.

Show code 
days_in_window <- function(start, end) as.integer(end - start) + 1

final_sizes <- function(R0, seed_date, n_seed, n_sims, cap = target_cases, k = k_sars) {
  # Cumulative infections on target_date in n_sims simulated epidemics.
  # Exact below `cap`; a value at or above `cap` means "at least cap".
  n_days <- days_in_window(seed_date, target_date)
  replicate(n_sims, {
    simulate_outbreak(R0, k, n_seed, n_days, max_cases = cap,
                      gt_shape = gt_shape, gt_rate = gt_rate)[n_days]
  })
}

proportion_reaching_target <- function(R0, seed_date, n_seed, n_sims) {
  mean(final_sizes(R0, seed_date, n_seed, n_sims) >= target_cases)
}

The one date the report did not give

The caption places the 40 zoonotic infections in December 2019 but gives no exact date. We test seeding dates from 20 November to 20 December at and choose the date for which the proportion reaching 4,000 infections by 18 January is closest to 50%. This calibrates our model to the report’s central estimate.

Show code 
set.seed(20200125)
n_sims_cal <- 1000
candidate_dates <- seq(as.Date("2019-11-20"), as.Date("2019-12-20"), by = "day")

calibration <- data.frame(
  candidate = candidate_dates,
  proportion_reaching = vapply(seq_along(candidate_dates), function(i) {
    proportion_reaching_target(R0_baseline, seed_date = candidate_dates[i],
                          n_seed = 40, n_sims = n_sims_cal)
  }, numeric(1))
)

seed_date <- calibration$candidate[which.min(abs(calibration$proportion_reaching - 0.5))]
seed_date
[1] "2019-12-14"
Show code 
show_dates <- seed_date + c(-14, -7, -3, 0, 3, 7, 14)
calibration %>%
  filter(candidate %in% show_dates) %>%
  mutate(candidate = fmt_date(candidate),
         proportion_reaching = fmt_pct(proportion_reaching)) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Seeding date", "Proportion reaching 4,000 by 18 Jan"),
               align = c("l", "r"))

The calibrated date is 14 December 2019, the only input tuned to the report’s result. The 40-seed central estimate therefore matches by construction. The endpoints and the 200-seed estimates provide comparisons that were not directly calibrated, although they use this fitted date.

The report counted cases by symptom onset; our model counts infections. An incubation period of roughly five days would place the seeds’ symptom onsets about five days after infection. The earliest onset in Wuhan’s first published clinical series was 1 December 2019. (5) Our fitted date is an effective timing parameter for this reconstruction, rather than an estimate of the spillover date.

Reproducing Figure 1

With that date fixed, we simulate 5,000 trajectories at through 25 January and summarise the daily counts.

Show code 
n_sims_fig <- 5000
n_days_fig <- days_in_window(seed_date, report_date)

trajectories <- replicate(n_sims_fig, {
  simulate_outbreak(R0_baseline, k_sars, n_seed = 40, n_days = n_days_fig,
                    gt_shape = gt_shape, gt_rate = gt_rate)
})

# Day 0 holds the 40 seeds plus any secondary infections that occur within
# the first day, so the count can slightly exceed 40.
stopifnot(dim(trajectories) == c(n_days_fig, n_sims_fig),
          all(trajectories[1, ] >= 40),
          all(diff(trajectories[, 1]) >= 0))
Show code 
dates_fig <- seed_date + (seq_len(n_days_fig) - 1)

band <- data.frame(
  date   = dates_fig,
  median = unname(apply(trajectories, 1, median)),
  lower  = unname(apply(trajectories, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025)),
  upper  = unname(apply(trajectories, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975))
)

at_target        <- trajectories[dates_fig == target_date, ]
median_at_target <- median(at_target)
proportion_at_target  <- mean(at_target >= target_cases)
c(median_on_18_jan = median_at_target, proportion_at_or_above_4000 = proportion_at_target)
           median_on_18_jan proportion_at_or_above_4000 
                  3852.0000                      0.4698

shown <- sample(n_sims_fig, 60)
sample_paths <- as.data.frame(trajectories[, shown])
sample_paths$date <- dates_fig
sample_paths <- pivot_longer(sample_paths, cols = -date,
                             names_to = "simulation", values_to = "cumulative")

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = band, aes(x = date, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
              fill = "grey82") +
  geom_line(data = sample_paths,
            aes(x = date, y = cumulative, group = simulation),
            colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = band, aes(x = date, y = median),
            colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = target_date, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = target_cases, linetype = "dotted") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, max(band$upper) * 1.02)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 week", labels = label_day_month) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = fmt_count) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cumulative infections",
       title = "Simulated epidemics in Wuhan: 40 zoonotic cases, R0 = 2.6",
       subtitle = "Median (red), 95% range (grey band), 60 of 5,000 individual trajectories (grey lines)")

On 18 January, the median is 3,852 infections, 47% of simulations reach 4,000, and the grey band spans 916 to 9,554. Identical assumptions produce widely different histories: some outbreaks remain small because early chains die out or large clusters occur late.

Why a proportion of simulations yields a confidence interval

The idea is to rule out values of that make the observed outbreak size implausible. For each candidate, we ask: would 4,000 cases be unusually large or unusually small?

Test each candidate value

Fix the seed count and timing, generation-time distribution and dispersion . Let be the simulated infection count on 18 January. For a candidate , reject it if either

The two tests rule out different explanations:

  • Too little transmission: fewer than 5% of epidemics reach 4,000 cases, so the observed outbreak is unusually large for this .
  • Too much transmission: fewer than 5% have 4,000 cases or fewer, so the observed outbreak is unusually small for this .

Keep the candidates that pass both tests. In this model, increasing shifts outbreak sizes upward, so the retained values form an interval. This construction is called test inversion. (6)

Keep the assumptions in view

  • Fixed inputs: the interval reflects random variation between epidemics under the chosen seed count, timing and transmission assumptions. Combining endpoints across scenarios does not automatically preserve the 90% coverage guarantee.

  • An estimated target: 4,000 was inferred from seven exported cases. Treating it as exact omits uncertainty in that inference. Imperial explored sensitivity by repeating the analysis at 1,000 and 9,700 cases.

  • Numerical error: for an estimated proportion from independent simulations, the estimated binomial standard error is

    With and , this gives

    In other words, about 0.49 percentage points. This measures random variation from the finite number of simulations. A finite grid adds interpolation error.

After comparing Table 1, we will check coverage by simulating epidemics at a known and counting how often their intervals contain it.

Reproducing the Table 1 estimates

We compute the proportion curve over an grid for 40 seeds, the baseline, and 200 seeds, the scenario that supplied the headline range’s lower endpoint.

Show code 
R0_grid     <- round(seq(0.8, 4.5, by = 0.1), 1)
n_sims_grid <- 2000

proportion_curve <- function(n_seed) {
  vapply(R0_grid, proportion_reaching_target, numeric(1),
         seed_date = seed_date, n_seed = n_seed, n_sims = n_sims_grid)
}

curves <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(n_seed = 40,  R0 = R0_grid, proportion_reaching = proportion_curve(40)),
  data.frame(n_seed = 200, R0 = R0_grid, proportion_reaching = proportion_curve(200))
)

We linearly interpolate between grid points to find the 5%, 50% and 95% crossings, then round to one decimal as the report did.

Show code 
R0_at_proportion <- function(R0, proportion, p) {
  # R0 at which the nondecreasing proportion curve first reaches p, by linear
  # interpolation between grid points. -Inf: already at or above p at the
  # smallest grid value. Inf: never reaches p within the grid.
  i <- which(proportion >= p)[1]
  if (is.na(i)) return(Inf)
  if (i == 1) return(-Inf)
  R0[i - 1] + (p - proportion[i - 1]) / (proportion[i] - proportion[i - 1]) * (R0[i] - R0[i - 1])
}

estimates <- curves %>%
  group_by(n_seed) %>%
  summarise(best_case  = R0_at_proportion(R0, proportion_reaching, 0.05),
            central    = R0_at_proportion(R0, proportion_reaching, 0.50),
            worst_case = R0_at_proportion(R0, proportion_reaching, 0.95),
            .groups = "drop")
estimates

2    200      1.50    1.69       1.94
Show code 
imperial <- data.frame(
  n_seed     = c(40, 200),
  best_case  = c(2.1, 1.5),
  central    = c(2.6, 1.7),
  worst_case = c(3.5, 2.0)
)

comparison <- bind_rows(mutate(imperial,  source = "Report 3, Table 1"),
                        mutate(estimates, source = "This simulation")) %>%
  arrange(n_seed, source) %>%
  mutate(across(c(best_case, central, worst_case), fmt1)) %>%
  select(n_seed, source, best_case, central, worst_case)

knitr::kable(comparison,
             col.names = c("Zoonotic cases", "Source", "Best case (5%)",
                           "Central (50%)", "Worst case (95%)"),
             align = c("r", "l", "r", "r", "r"))
Show code 
seed_levels <- c("40 zoonotic cases", "200 zoonotic cases")

curves_plot <- curves %>%
  mutate(seeds = factor(paste(n_seed, "zoonotic cases"), levels = seed_levels))

imperial_points <- imperial %>%
  pivot_longer(-n_seed, names_to = "estimate", values_to = "R0") %>%
  mutate(proportion_reaching = unname(c(best_case = 0.05, central = 0.5,
                                   worst_case = 0.95)[estimate]),
         seeds = factor(paste(n_seed, "zoonotic cases"), levels = seed_levels))

ggplot(curves_plot, aes(x = R0, y = proportion_reaching, colour = seeds)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), linetype = "dotted",
             colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = imperial_points, shape = 4, size = 3.2, stroke = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("40 zoonotic cases"  = "firebrick",
                                 "200 zoonotic cases" = "steelblue"),
                      name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = fmt_pct, breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.25)) +
  labs(x = expression(R[0]),
       y = "Proportion of simulations \n reaching 4,000 infections by 18 Jan",
       title = "How the best-case, central and worst-case estimates are read off",
       subtitle = "Dotted lines: 5%, 50% and 95%. Crosses: Report 3, Table 1") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

For 40 seeds, our endpoints are 2.1 and 3.3, compared with the report’s 2.1 and 3.5. For 200 seeds, we obtain 1.5, 1.7 and 1.9, compared with 1.5, 1.7 and 2.0. The report’s headline 1.5–3.5 joins the best case for 200 seeds to the worst case for 40.

Exact agreement is unlikely: rounding, Monte Carlo error, and our choices about seed timing and generation-time shape all affect the estimates. These comparisons assess the reconstruction as a whole; they cannot isolate the cause of a discrepancy.

The interval narrows from 40 to 200 seeds because more independent chains average out individual superspreading events. Imperial also obtained a narrower range by assuming less heterogeneity, , without greatly changing the central estimate. (3)

Checking the coverage claim

The approximate interval interpretation suggests coverage near 90% under the fixed model. To check it, we simulate outbreak-size distributions on a coarser grid, recording sizes up to a cap. We then generate epidemics at and build each interval from the estimated 5% and 95% crossings of the proportion reaching its observed size.

Sizes at or above the cap are treated as equal to it. Capping can affect coverage for those epidemics, so their proportion bounds the resulting error and is reported below.

Show code 
R0_true     <- 2.6
n_obs       <- 400
n_sims_cov  <- 1000
size_cap    <- 30000
R0_grid_cov <- round(seq(1.0, 4.6, by = 0.2), 1)

# Full distribution of sizes on 18 January at each grid value, 40 seeds
sizes_cov <- lapply(R0_grid_cov, function(R0) {
  final_sizes(R0, seed_date = seed_date, n_seed = 40,
              n_sims = n_sims_cov, cap = size_cap)
})
proportion_at <- function(sizes, n) vapply(sizes, function(s) mean(s >= n), numeric(1))

# Sizes on 18 January of epidemics generated under the known R0
observed <- final_sizes(R0_true, seed_date = seed_date, n_seed = 40, n_sims = n_obs, cap = size_cap)
proportion_at_cap <- mean(observed >= size_cap)
observed     <- pmin(observed, size_cap)

interval_for <- function(n) {
  S <- proportion_at(sizes_cov, n)
  c(lower  = R0_at_proportion(R0_grid_cov, S, 0.05),
    centre = R0_at_proportion(R0_grid_cov, S, 0.50),
    upper  = R0_at_proportion(R0_grid_cov, S, 0.95))
}

intervals <- as.data.frame(t(vapply(observed, interval_for, numeric(3))))
intervals$observed <- observed
intervals$covered  <- intervals$lower <= R0_true & intervals$upper >= R0_true

c(coverage     = mean(intervals$covered),
  missed_below = mean(intervals$upper < R0_true),
  missed_above = mean(intervals$lower > R0_true),
  proportion_at_cap = proportion_at_cap)
         coverage      missed_below      missed_above proportion_at_cap 
            0.895             0.060             0.045             0.000
Show code 
n_show <- 100
shown_intervals <- intervals[seq_len(n_show), ] %>%
  arrange(observed) %>%
  mutate(rank   = row_number(),
         lower_plot  = pmax(lower,  min(R0_grid_cov)),
         upper_plot  = pmin(upper,  max(R0_grid_cov)),
         centre_plot = pmin(pmax(centre, min(R0_grid_cov)), max(R0_grid_cov)),
         status = ifelse(covered, "Contains the true R0", "Misses the true R0"))

ggplot(shown_intervals) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = R0_true, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower_plot, xend = upper_plot, y = rank, yend = rank,
                   colour = status), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = centre_plot, y = rank, colour = status), size = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Contains the true R0" = "steelblue",
                                 "Misses the true R0"   = "firebrick"),
                      name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = range(R0_grid_cov)) +
  labs(x = expression(R[0]),
       y = "Simulated epidemics, ordered by size on 18 January",
       title = "Intervals built by the report's rule from 100 epidemics with R0 = 2.6",
       subtitle = "Segment: best case to worst case. Dot: central estimate.") +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        axis.text.y = element_blank())

Across 400 epidemics, 90% of intervals contain the true value; 6% fall entirely below it and 4% entirely above. The nominal proportions are 90%, 5% and 5%. At this sample size, coverage near 90% has a binomial standard error of about 1.5 percentage points, in addition to grid and simulation error. 0% of epidemics reached the cap. Misses correspond to unusually small or large outbreaks under the true model.

The intervals are asymmetric, as in Table 1. Large outbreaks tend to produce longer intervals because the right-skewed size distribution allows a broad range of values to generate them.

The Bayesian counterpart: Riou and Althaus

A related analysis appeared in Eurosurveillance onOn 30 January 2020, five days after Report 3. The authors used the same model class but averaged over uncertain inputs and accepted a range of outbreak sizes. (7)

The model. Offspring counts are negative binomial with mean and dispersion . Generation times are gamma-distributed with shape 2 and mean , giving greater relative spread than our SARS-based distribution. Epidemics with index cases are assembled from single-chain simulations sampled with replacement and assigned staggered start dates.

Priors on a grid. They assigned equal prior weight to the parameter grid points below, with spaced uniformly on a logarithmic scale.

Parameter Range Grid
0.8 to 5.0 22 equidistant values
Dispersion 0.01 to 10 20 values, equidistant on a log10 scale
Mean generation time 7 to 14 days 8 equidistant values
Index cases 1 to 50 6 equidistant values
Onset date of each index case 20 November to 4 December 2019 Uniform, drawn separately for each index case

They simulated 1,000 chains for each of 3,520 combinations of , and —3.52 million chains—and assembled 2,112,000 epidemics across the grid including .

Acceptance against Report 2’s range. They retained epidemics with 1,000–9,700 cumulative infections on 18 January, using Report 2’s uncertainty range. Parameter combinations were weighted by their proportion of accepted simulations to approximate a posterior. (7) This is a form of rejection-based approximate Bayesian computation. (8) The acceptance window allows uncertainty in outbreak size, although it does not explicitly model the exported-case observations.

Results. The posterior median of was 2.2, with a 90% highest-density interval of 1.4–3.8. For , the median was 0.54 and the 90% interval was 0.014–6.95: outbreak size alone weakly constrained superspreading. The authors found transmissibility compatible with SARS and pandemic influenza and warned of possible global spread. Their analysis still depended on Report 2’s range and its assumption that all infected travellers from Wuhan had been detected. (7)

How the two analyses relate.

  • Both use a negative binomial branching process with gamma generation times. Adapting our simulator to draw inputs from the Bern grids and apply their acceptance window would give a related Bayesian analysis.
  • Imperial fixed uncertain inputs and produced conditional intervals for each scenario. Riou and Althaus averaged across inputs and accepted outbreak sizes, producing a marginal posterior for .
  • Their estimates overlap substantially: 2.2 (1.4–3.8), compared with Imperial’s baseline 2.6 (2.1–3.5) and headline range of 1.5–3.5. Different seed, timing and acceptance assumptions can shift the results; this comparison alone cannot explain the lower median.
  • The broad posterior for shows how little one cumulative count reveals about transmission heterogeneity. Imperial supplied that information by analogy with SARS.

Reading the headline estimate carefully

The preferred scenario gave and endpoints of 2.1–3.5, conditional on 40 seed cases and the 4,000-case target. The headline 1.5–3.5 also spanned alternative seed counts; outbreak-size and transmission assumptions were varied separately. (3)

That headline range is not a single 95% confidence interval. It combines approximately 90% conditional intervals across scenarios. Reading it requires asking which observations constrain the estimate, which assumptions support it, and how changing those assumptions changes the result.

What the result meant for public health

Imperial concluded that sustained human-to-human transmission was occurring and that control required blocking well over 60% of transmission. Imperial’s report summary

Under a simple proportional reduction, preventing a fraction of transmission gives

For , bringing the effective reproduction number below one requires

item.title: From Exported Cases to Outbreak Size: Imperial’s First Two COVID-19 Reports
item.dc:creator: Jong-Hoon Kim
item.description:
Three travellers, thousands of cases?

In January 2020, three confirmed cases detected in Thailand and Japan offered a window into a poorly observed outbreak in Wuhan. Imperial College London’s first COVID-19 report estimated 1,723 [95% CI: 427 – 4,471] clinically comparable cases with symptom onset by 12 January 2020. Five days later, its second report used seven exported cases to estimate approximately 4,000 cases [uncertainty range: 1,000 – 9,700] with onset by 18 January. (1,2)

We first work through the Imperial reports: their observation model, travel probability, estimates and uncertainty intervals. We then examine the probability approximation and compare the formulae and assumptions with those of Nishiura and colleagues.

Imperial’s observation model

Let be the unknown source count of relevant cases, the observed number detected abroad, and the probability that any one relevant source case is detected abroad. If cases have independent, equal observation probabilities,

Equating the observed count to its expectation (the method of moments approach) gives a ratio estimate that scales the observed exports up to a source-case total:

For the maximum likelihood approach, we specify a probability distribution for and choose the parameter that makes the observed count most probable. Under , the likelihood is maximized when the mean equals , which gives . In this approximation, we allow to vary continuously, so the estimate can be fractional. The exact binomial model restricts to integers at least . For , its unique maximum likelihood estimate is when is not an integer. If and is an integer, both and maximize the likelihood; our code returns the latter. For zero observed exports, the maximum is at .

NoteWhy do you round down to get the MLE?

If , the unique binomial MLE is 37. The word “larger” applies only when two totals tie: if , both 37 and 38 maximize the likelihood, and our convention returns 38. A tie does not assign a 50% probability to each total. It means that both give the same probability to the observed data.

Matching the expected count as closely as possible does not always maximize the probability of the exact observed count. For example, suppose we observe one detection and . Then , which is closer to three than two, but:

Show code 
candidate_totals <- c(2, 3)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  total_N = candidate_totals,
  expected_detections = candidate_totals * 0.36,
  probability_of_one_detection = dbinom(1, size = candidate_totals, prob = 0.36)
), digits = 6)
total_N expected_detections probability_of_one_detection
2 0.72 0.460800
3 1.08 0.442368

With two cases, the probability of exactly one detection is 0.4608, whereas the probability of zero detections is . Adding a third case can help produce exactly one detection if the original two produced zero; it can also spoil an outcome of exactly one by adding another detection. Both changes require detecting the third case, with the same probability 0.36. Because one detection was initially more likely than zero, more probability moves away from exactly one than moves into it. Thus the likelihood decreases from 0.4608 to 0.442368.

More generally, comparing adjacent totals gives

This ratio is above one when , equals one when , and is below one when . That explains both rounding down for a noninteger ratio and the tie at an integer ratio. For the Imperial baseline, , so the unique total- binomial MLE is 1,726. These neighboring-count distinctions are tiny compared with the uncertainty interval.

Constructing the historical probability

The reports use with the following inputs. The product is not automatically bounded by one. An exact probability under a specified travel model uses the complement of the probability of no travel during the window, and must also account for detection after travel. We derive these steps below. (1,2)

Symbol Meaning Baseline and units
Outbound international passenger flow 3,301 passengers/day
Airport catchment population 19,000,000 people
Mean infection-to-detection opportunity window 10 days

The window combines infection-to-onset and onset-to-detection time. The reports used an approximate 5–6-day incubation period and a further 4–5 days before detection. They assumed exported cases would remain abroad long enough to be detected. (1)

Dividing passenger flow by population gives a per-person daily travel quantity. Treating that quantity as a case’s travel probability requires assumptions about who travels, repeat trips, and whether cases resemble the catchment population. Under complete detection abroad, the baseline arithmetic is:

The functions for the Imperial examples are defined in the expandable block below. This base-R teaching code assumes inputs follow the units and domains described in the text; routine type and input-validation checks are omitted. Brief checks remain where a calculation would be undefined or an interval could be cut short. Confidence limits are calculated by checking a grid of candidate case counts directly. The default upper limit, max_N = 20000, covers the examples below; increase it if an interval reaches the grid boundary. Run the definitions before the examples.

Show all required base-R functions 
# Observation probability; inputs use passengers/day, people, and days.
export_probability <- function(daily_travellers, catchment_population,
                               window_days, detection = 1,
                               travel_multiplier = 1,
                               approximation = c("linear", "poisson")) {
  # Choose "linear" or "poisson"; the default is "linear".
  approximation <- match.arg(approximation)

  # Accumulate the per-person daily travel quantity over the window.
  # travel_multiplier = 1 assumes cases travel at the population-average rate.
  # Under the constant-rate model, exposure = travel rate * window duration.
  # Exposure is not itself guaranteed to be a probability: it can exceed 1.
  exposure <- daily_travellers / catchment_population * window_days * travel_multiplier

  # This is an if/else expression: "==" compares; "<-" assigns the result.
  # If approximation is "linear", set travel_prob to exposure.
  # Otherwise ("poisson"), set it to 1 - exp(-exposure).
  # The second formula is exact for constant-rate Poisson travel over a
  # fixed window; the first approximates it when exposure is small.
  # expm1(x) means exp(x) - 1, computed accurately even when x is near zero.
  # Hence -expm1(-exposure) = 1 - exp(-exposure), without losing accuracy
  # through subtraction of nearly equal numbers. For example, in R,
  # exp(1e-20) - 1 gives 0, whereas expm1(1e-20) preserves about 1e-20.
  # At exposure = 0.1, the linear result is 0.1 and the Poisson result 0.09516.
  travel_prob <- if (approximation == "linear") exposure else -expm1(-exposure)
  if (travel_prob > 1) stop("Linear travel probability exceeds 1; review inputs or use an appropriate travel model.", call. = FALSE)

  # Travel and overseas detection are separate events. Multiply by the
  # probability of detection conditional on having traveled in the window.
  p <- detection * travel_prob
  p
}

# Assume x is a nonnegative integer, 0 < p <= 1, and 0 < conf_level < 1.
# Check candidate source totals directly; no search helpers are needed.
# max_N is the largest total to examine (20,000 covers this post's examples).
# Increase max_N if the confidence interval reaches that boundary.
infer_binomial_size <- function(x, p, conf_level = 0.95,
                                interval = c("exact", "lr"), max_N = 20000) {
  interval <- match.arg(interval)
  # A noninteger x/p has one MLE: floor(x/p), not the nearest integer.
  # For 0 < p < 1 and x > 0, an integer x/p ties with x/p - 1; return x/p.
  estimate <- floor(x / p)
  if (max_N <= estimate) stop("Increase max_N beyond the estimated total.")
  N <- seq.int(x, max_N)

  if (interval == "exact") {
    # Keep totals for which neither binomial tail is smaller than alpha/2.
    alpha <- 1 - conf_level
    keep <- pbinom(x - 1, size = N, prob = p, lower.tail = FALSE) >= alpha / 2 &
            pbinom(x, size = N, prob = p) >= alpha / 2
    method <- "Exact equal-tailed"
  } else {
    # Keep totals whose log likelihood is sufficiently close to its maximum.
    log_likelihood <- dbinom(x, size = N, prob = p, log = TRUE)
    best <- dbinom(x, size = estimate, prob = p, log = TRUE)
    keep <- 2 * (best - log_likelihood) <= qchisq(conf_level, df = 1)
    method <- "Asymptotic likelihood-ratio"
  }

  if (tail(keep, 1)) stop("Increase max_N: the interval reaches the grid boundary.")
  limits <- range(N[keep])
  data.frame(x = x, p = p, estimate = estimate,
             lower = limits[1], upper = limits[2],
             conf_level = conf_level, method = method)
}

# Simulate binomial observations for a fixed hypothetical source count.
simulate_export_counts <- function(total_cases, p, nsim = 1000) {
  stats::rbinom(nsim, size = total_cases, prob = p)
}
Show code 
F <- 3301                 # passengers/day
M <- 19000000            # people
D <- 10                  # days from infection to detection
p <- export_probability(F, M, D)
data.frame(p = p, cases_per_detection = 1 / p,
           three_exports = 3 / p, seven_exports = 7 / p)
            p cases_per_detection three_exports seven_exports
1 0.001737368            575.5832      1726.749      4029.082

The probability is approximately 0.00173737, or 0.174%. The ratio estimates are 1,726.75 and 4,029.08. These illustrate the scale; they are not exact reproductions of the reports’ printed estimates. The function definitions above support the Imperial examples; the package comparison defines its additional function alongside the worked example.

What the reports actually estimated

Item Report 1 Report 2
Publication 17 January 2020 22 January 2020
Exported cases 3 7
Symptom onset through 12 January 18 January
Published baseline estimate 1,723 4,000
Published baseline 95% interval 427–4,471 1,700–7,800
Headline scenario envelope — 1,000–9,700

Report 2’s envelope spans the confidence intervals for its baseline, smaller-catchment, and shorter-window scenarios. It expresses sensitivity to selected assumptions alongside statistical uncertainty. The report also explicitly warns against estimating an epidemic growth rate from the two point estimates: reporting delays, onset information, and sparse observations prevent that interpretation. (2)

Why a negative-binomial expression appears

Report 2 introduces the negative-binomial distribution in its methods section as follows:

Confidence intervals can be calculated from the observation that the number of cases detected overseas, X, is binomially distributed as Bin(p,N), where p = probability any one case will be detected overseas, and N is the total number of cases. N is therefore a negative binomially distributed function of X. (2)

Both methods sections mention a negative-binomial likelihood without specifying all implementation details. The derivation below explains the algebraic relationship behind this statement and distinguishes a likelihood from a probability distribution over the unknown total. First distinguish the total number of cases, , from the number not detected overseas, :

With three observed exports, and describe the same possible outbreak. They are two ways to label its size, not competing estimates of the same count.

Start with the binomial likelihood. Once we observe , we hold and fixed and compare possible totals :

Substituting changes only the label for the unknown count:

Now compare this with the negative-binomial probability of failures before the th success:

Setting makes this expression equal to the binomial likelihood multiplied by :

Why rather than ? The negative-binomial formula contains in its binomial coefficient. To match the observed count there, we need . This is an algebraic match: with three observed exports, R therefore uses size = 4, but we have not observed a fourth export or sampled until one appeared.

We have not changed the sampling model for the observed exports. It remains . The negative binomial formula appears because it is proportional to that likelihood when written in terms of . The extra factor normalizes the values so that .

The identity can be checked directly in base R:

Show code 
x_observed <- 3
p_known <- 3301 * 10 / 19000000
k_candidates <- c(1722, 1723, 1724)  # Cases not detected overseas.
N_candidates <- k_candidates + x_observed  # Total cases.

binomial_likelihood <- dbinom(x_observed, size = N_candidates, prob = p_known)
# size = x + 1 matches the formula; it does not imply a fourth observed export.
negative_binomial_mass <- dnbinom(k_candidates, size = x_observed + 1,
                                 prob = p_known)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  total_N = N_candidates, not_detected_overseas_k = k_candidates,
  p_times_L = p_known * binomial_likelihood,
  g = negative_binomial_mass
), digits = 9)
total_N not_detected_overseas_k p_times_L g
1725 1722 0.000389581 0.000389581
1726 1723 0.000389582 0.000389582
1727 1724 0.000389582 0.000389582
Show code 
# TRUE means the two expressions agree to numerical precision.
isTRUE(all.equal(negative_binomial_mass, p_known * binomial_likelihood))
[1] TRUE

Multiplying every likelihood by the same positive constant preserves the ranking of candidate totals and all likelihood ratios. Consequently, the maximum at corresponds to the maximum at . An interval for must likewise have added to both endpoints to express it as an interval for , when using the same interval procedure.

For example, the constant cancels when comparing any two candidate counts:

The reconstruction below uses these likelihood ratios; it does not calculate negative-binomial probability quantiles or Bayesian credible intervals.

The inferred reconstruction matching the reports uses the mode of :

This produces 1,723 for three exports, matching Report 1’s printed total. However, in the algebra above, 1,723 represents , and the corresponding total is 1,726. Matching the printed number does not establish how the authors implemented their calculation or justify treating as in a new analysis.

Reconstructing the reports’ likelihood-ratio intervals

With fixed, we compare candidate case counts by how likely they make the observed exports. Write . A likelihood-ratio interval retains candidates satisfying

The endpoints are where this log-likelihood drop reaches the cutoff. The foundational reference for the chi-squared likelihood-ratio approximation is Wilks (1938). Under suitable regularity conditions and in large samples, twice the log-likelihood drop has an approximate chi-squared distribution, with one degree of freedom when testing one scalar parameter. Retaining the parameter values that the test does not reject gives a likelihood-ratio confidence interval. (3)

This is an approximate 95% confidence interval. With few observed exports and an integer-valued unknown total, Wilks’s general result does not by itself establish exact 95% coverage; the exact binomial interval below uses a separate construction.

The following inferred reconstruction calculates an interval for , uses a cutoff rounded to 3.84, and rounds continuous endpoints. It reproduces Report 1’s printed result, but the reports do not establish that these were their exact numerical conventions. (1,2)

Show code 
exports <- 3
p_interval <- 3301 * 10 / 19000000

# At integer k, this is dnbinom(k, size = exports + 1,
#                             prob = p_interval, log = TRUE).
# It equals the binomial log likelihood at N = k + exports, plus log(p).
# That constant cancels when we subtract log likelihoods below.
# lchoose also permits continuous endpoint searches.
log_likelihood <- function(k) {
  lchoose(k + exports, exports) +
    (exports + 1) * log(p_interval) + k * log1p(-p_interval)
}
k_hat <- floor(exports * (1 - p_interval) / p_interval)
cutoff <- round(qchisq(0.95, df = 1), 2)
boundary <- function(k) {
  2 * (log_likelihood(k_hat) - log_likelihood(k)) - cutoff
}

# Search brackets sufficient for the report's baseline inputs.
report_lower <- uniroot(boundary, c(0, k_hat))$root
report_upper <- uniroot(boundary, c(k_hat, 20000))$root
round(c(estimate = k_hat, lower = report_lower, upper = report_upper))
estimate    lower    upper 
    1723      427     4471

This gives 1,723 (427–4,471). Repeating with seven exports gives approximately 4,022 (1,726–7,780), which rounds to Report 2’s 4,000 (1,700–7,800) at its printed precision. These reconstructed values describe in our derivation. To express them as total cases , add the observed exports to the estimate and both endpoints.

Report 2’s broader uncertainty range is a separate operation. Its baseline, smaller-catchment and shorter-window intervals are 1,700–7,800, 1,000–4,500 and 2,200–9,700. Taking the smallest lower endpoint and largest upper endpoint gives 1,000–9,700. This sensitivity envelope explores selected assumptions about ; it has no newly established 95% coverage interpretation. (2)

Direct binomial likelihood and exact tail inversion

For the total source count, use

Applying the likelihood-ratio rule directly to integer gives an estimate of 1,726 and interval 431–4,474 for three exports. The expressions and give the same relative support to each possible outbreak: one labels it by , while the other labels it by . Adding three to the reconstruction’s rounded endpoints gives 430–4,474. The remaining one-case difference in the lower limit comes from the numerical conventions: the reconstruction rounds continuous endpoints and uses 3.84, whereas the direct calculation retains accepted integers and uses the unrounded chi-squared cutoff. It does not reflect a different model for the observed exports.

Show code 
binomial_lr <- infer_binomial_size(3, p_interval, interval = "lr")
binomial_exact <- infer_binomial_size(3, p_interval, interval = "exact")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  calculation = c("Reconstruction matching Report 1 (k = N - x)",
                  "Direct binomial LR (total N)",
                  "Exact equal-tailed binomial (total N)"),
  estimate = c(k_hat, binomial_lr$estimate, binomial_exact$estimate),
  lower = c(round(report_lower), binomial_lr$lower, binomial_exact$lower),
  upper = c(round(report_upper), binomial_lr$upper, binomial_exact$upper)
), caption = "Three exports and the same fixed observation probability.")
Three exports and the same fixed observation probability.
calculation estimate lower upper
Reconstruction matching Report 1 (k = N - x) 1723 427 4471
Direct binomial LR (total N) 1726 431 4474
Exact equal-tailed binomial (total N) 1726 357 5043

The exact equal-tailed interval, 357–5,043, uses a different interval construction: exact binomial tail probabilities instead of the approximate chi-squared likelihood-ratio cutoff.

With interval = "exact", infer_binomial_size() inverts both binomial tails to construct this equal-tailed confidence interval. For , it retains integer values satisfying

Show code 
conditional <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 3, 7), function(x) {
  infer_binomial_size(x, p, interval = "exact")
}))
knitr::kable(conditional[c("x", "estimate", "lower", "upper")],
             col.names = c("Exports", "Total-N MLE", "95% lower", "95% upper"),
             caption = "New total-N binomial analysis, conditional on fixed p; not the published intervals.")
New total-N binomial analysis, conditional on fixed p; not the published intervals.
Exports Total-N MLE 95% lower 95% upper
0 0 0 2121
3 1726 357 5043
7 4029 1622 8297

These intervals have at least nominal coverage under the stated model with known . They exclude uncertainty in passenger flow, catchment size, delay distributions, and detection completeness. Zero exports yield an estimate of zero but a positive upper limit: the absence of detections does not establish the absence of cases.

Confidence intervals with established R packages

We can check our calculations with bbmle, stats4, and stats. For a direct comparison between implementations, we first give all three packages the same Poisson approximation, , with known and continuous positive .

Show the package comparison function 
# Install once if needed; this commented line does not run when rendering:
# install.packages("bbmle")
# Compare likelihood-ratio intervals under X ~ Poisson(N * p).
# Inputs: positive observed count x, known detection probability p, confidence level.
# Output: estimates and interval endpoints on the total-case scale N.
# This teaching example requires x > 0; log(N) has no finite MLE when x = 0.
compare_poisson_intervals <- function(x, p, conf_level = 0.95) {
  # Optimize log(N) so N stays positive; this model allows noninteger N.
  nll <- function(log_N) -dpois(x, lambda = exp(log_N) * p, log = TRUE)
  log_N_hat <- log(x / p)

  # Our direct likelihood-ratio calculation, now using the SAME Poisson model.
  boundary <- function(log_N) {
    2 * (nll(log_N) - nll(log_N_hat)) - qchisq(conf_level, 1)
  }
  # These brackets cover the examples x = 3 and x = 7 at 95% confidence.
  manual_ci <- exp(c(
    uniroot(boundary, c(log_N_hat - 10, log_N_hat), tol = 1e-10)$root,
    uniroot(boundary, c(log_N_hat, log_N_hat + 10), tol = 1e-10)$root
  ))

  fit_bbmle <- bbmle::mle2(nll, start = list(log_N = log_N_hat))
  # "spline" profiles the likelihood; "quad" would give a Wald approximation.
  # Use the S4 generic in stats4 for mle2 and mle objects.
  ci_bbmle <- exp(stats4::confint(fit_bbmle, level = conf_level, method = "spline",
                                         del = 0.05, maxsteps = 100))

  fit_stats4 <- stats4::mle(nll, start = list(log_N = log_N_hat))
  ci_stats4 <- exp(stats4::confint(stats4::profile(fit_stats4, del = 0.05, maxsteps = 100),
                                 level = conf_level))

  # log(E[X]) = log(N) + log(p): log(p) is a known offset.
  fit_glm <- stats::glm(x ~ 1 + offset(log(p)), family = poisson())
  ci_glm <- exp(stats::confint(stats::profile(fit_glm, test = "LRT", del = 0.05,
                                              maxsteps = 100), level = conf_level))

  limits <- rbind(manual_ci, ci_bbmle, ci_stats4, ci_glm)
  data.frame(
    method = c("Manual Poisson LR", "bbmle profile", "stats4 profile", "Poisson GLM profile"),
    estimate = c(x / p, exp(stats4::coef(fit_bbmle)),
                 exp(stats4::coef(fit_stats4)), exp(coef(fit_glm))),
    lower = limits[, 1], upper = limits[, 2], row.names = NULL
  )
}
Show code 
# Use the same report inputs for every calculation.
package_intervals <- compare_poisson_intervals(3, p_interval)
comparison <- rbind(
  package_intervals,
  data.frame(method = "Our integer-binomial LR",
             binomial_lr[c("estimate", "lower", "upper")]),
  data.frame(method = "Our exact binomial tails",
             binomial_exact[c("estimate", "lower", "upper")])
)

             caption = "Three exports: Poisson package intervals compared with our calculations.")

knitr::kable(compare_poisson_intervals(7, p_interval), digits = 2,

For three exports, the Poisson calculations give approximately 1,726.75 cases (429.42–4,477.63). In validation for three and seven exports, the package endpoints differ from our direct Poisson roots by less than 0.05 cases. Agreement checks the numerical calculation, not the coverage of this approximate interval. All use the likelihood-ratio principle discussed above. (3)

Our integer-binomial LR interval, 431–4,474, differs because it uses a different likelihood and integer candidates. The exact binomial interval, 357–5,043, also uses a different interval construction. The package examples are new Poisson analyses, not reproductions of Imperial’s printed negative-binomial calculation. A continuous optimizer cannot directly vary the size argument of dbinom() over noninteger totals; the integer-grid calculation remains appropriate for our direct binomial analysis.

All these intervals hold fixed. They therefore exclude uncertainty in travel flow, the opportunity window, and overseas detection. The relationship between the Imperial and Nishiura point-estimate formulae is explained below.

From escape probability to overseas detection

A daily probability multiplied by a duration can exceed one. The escape-probability calculation shows why this product is only a first-order approximation.

A fixed window: first calculate the probability of no travel

Let be the daily probability of international travel, conditional on not yet having travelled. First suppose the available window is exactly whole days. If that conditional probability stays constant, the probability of remaining without travel for the entire window is

This is the no-travel, or escape, probability: the case escapes the travel event on every day. Its complement is the probability of travelling before detection ends the opportunity window:

This expression is exact under the stated daily travel model and always lies between zero and one. Travel and overseas detection are separate events: if is the probability of detection conditional on travel during this window, then . The baseline calculation assumes for cases meeting the reports’ clinical definition. Expanding it shows where the approximation comes from:

Keeping only the first-order term gives the report’s multiplication when . The first row below uses the reports’ baseline , , and , taken directly from the R variables defined above. For this comparison, the exact daily calculation treats the window as fixed at days; the reports themselves specify a mean window.

Report inputs and illustrative comparisons. The baseline uses d = D; exact travel probability is 1 minus the no-travel probability. Dashes mean no passenger flow or population was specified.
Scenario (passengers/day) (people) (days) First order Exact
Report baseline 3,301 19,000,000 0.00017374 10 0.00173737 0.00173601
Illustration - - 0.00100000 10 0.01000000 0.00995512
Illustration - - 0.05000000 10 0.50000000 0.40126306
Illustration - - 0.20000000 10 2.00000000 0.89262582

At the report baseline, the first-order probability is approximately 0.00173737 and the exact daily-model probability is 0.00173601. For the illustrative rows, also gives an excellent approximation; noticeably overstates the probability, and gives a product above one. The exact calculation remains bounded in each case.

Nishiura et al. (2020)

Nishiura and colleagues also estimate outbreak size from detected exports, travel volume, a source population, and an opportunity window. Their calculation first estimates an infection risk and then multiplies it by the source population. Imperial instead first calculates the probability of detecting a source case overseas and then divides the observed exports by that probability. With matching inputs, these two routes give the same ratio estimate. Their different statistical interpretations still matter for uncertainty. (1,2,4)

The papers use for different probabilities. To keep them distinct, retain for Imperial’s overseas-detection probability and use for Nishiura’s source-population infection risk. Likewise, use for the source population throughout; Nishiura calls that population .

item.title: Nash Equilibrium, Starting Simple
item.dc:creator: Jong-Hoon Kim
item.description:
1 Why this matters

Vaccination coverage is not a parameter we set; it is the aggregate outcome of many decisions, each made by an agent who responds to what everyone else is doing. The mathematical object that describes where such mutually-responsive decisions settle is the Nash equilibrium (1). For a single well-mixed population, Bauch and Earn showed that voluntary vaccination settles at a Nash equilibrium strictly below the herd-immunity threshold (2) — a point epidemiologists had raised well before game theory entered the field (3). I worked through that single-population game in an earlier post.

This post starts one step earlier — what a Nash equilibrium actually is, using nothing more than a 2×2 table — and then goes one step further: what happens when there are two populations coupled by travel or shared borders, each choosing its own coverage. This is the setting that matters for real vaccination strategy: districts within a country, or neighboring countries deciding on cholera or typhoid vaccination campaigns whose benefits spill across the border (4). The punchline is that the free-rider problem operates at two levels at once: individuals free-ride on their neighbors, and populations free-ride on each other.

2 A Nash equilibrium in one table

Strip away everything continuous. Two neighboring health departments, A and B, each face one binary choice: fund a vaccination Campaign (C) or Not (N). A campaign costs 4 (in some currency of budget units). Epidemic costs depend on what both do, because transmission crosses the border:

  • If both run campaigns, the outbreak is suppressed: no epidemic cost.
  • If one runs a campaign, transmission is reduced everywhere, but incompletely: each department suffers epidemic cost 3.
  • If neither runs one, each suffers epidemic cost 8.

Each department pays its own campaign cost plus its own epidemic cost. Writing total costs as (A’s cost, B’s cost):

B: Campaign B: No campaign
A: Campaign (4, 4) (7, 3)
A: No campaign (3, 7) (8, 8)

A best response is the cheapest choice given what the other player does. Check A’s best responses:

  • If B campaigns, A pays 4 by campaigning or 3 by abstaining → best response: N. A free-rides on B’s spillover protection.
  • If B abstains, A pays 7 by campaigning or 8 by abstaining → best response: C. Facing an unchecked epidemic, even a solo campaign pays for itself.

A Nash equilibrium is a pair of choices in which each player is best-responding to the other — so no one can gain by unilaterally switching. Here there are two pure-strategy equilibria: (C, N) and (N, C). In each, exactly one department pays for a campaign and the other free-rides, and neither can do better by changing only its own choice. (There is also a mixed equilibrium in which each campaigns with probability 1/2 — Nash’s theorem guarantees at least one equilibrium always exists once mixing is allowed (1).)

Notice what is not an equilibrium: (C, C), the outcome with the lowest total cost (8, versus 10 in either free-rider equilibrium and 16 with no campaigns). The socially best outcome is unstable because each player, holding the other’s choice fixed, gains by defecting. That divergence between equilibrium and optimum is the entire story of vaccination games; the rest of this post just replaces the 2×2 table with epidemic dynamics.

3 One population, continuous strategies

Now let the strategy be continuous: each individual in a large well-mixed population decides whether to vaccinate before an epidemic, and the population-level outcome is a coverage . Let be the cost of vaccination relative to the cost of infection (so ), and let be the probability that an unvaccinated individual is eventually infected when coverage is .

For an SIR-type epidemic with a perfect vaccine, is the final size among the unvaccinated, which solves

and once exceeds the herd-immunity threshold .

The logic of the 2×2 table carries over directly. If , an unvaccinated individual gains by vaccinating, so coverage rises; if , a vaccinated individual would have preferred not to, so coverage falls. The interior Nash equilibrium is the indifference point (2):

Since requires , the equilibrium always sits below : voluntary vaccination never reaches herd immunity.

library(ggplot2)

# Final size among the unvaccinated at coverage p (perfect vaccine)
attack_rate <- function(p, R0) {
  R_eff <- R0 * (1 - p)
  if (R_eff <= 1) return(0)
  uniroot(function(z) z - (1 - exp(-R_eff * z)),
          interval = c(1e-9, 1), tol = 1e-12)$root
}

R0 <- 2.5   # e.g., a moderately transmissible respiratory pathogen
r  <- 0.2   # vaccination cost relative to infection cost

p_H    <- 1 - 1 / R0
p_nash <- uniroot(function(p) attack_rate(p, R0) - r,
                  interval = c(0, p_H - 1e-6))$root
round(c(nash = p_nash, herd_immunity = p_H), 3)
         nash herd_immunity 
        0.554         0.600

With and , voluntary coverage settles at 0.554 — below the herd-immunity threshold of 0.6, and stably so: any campaign that pushes coverage above lowers the infection risk below , and the incentive to vaccinate evaporates.

p_grid <- seq(0, 0.7, by = 0.002)
df <- data.frame(p = p_grid,
                 risk = sapply(p_grid, attack_rate, R0 = R0))

ggplot(df, aes(p, risk)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = r, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = p_nash, linetype = "dotted", color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = p_H, linetype = "dotted", color = "firebrick") +
  annotate("point", x = p_nash, y = r, size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  annotate("text", x = p_nash - 0.015, y = 0.45,
           label = sprintf("Nash equilibrium\np* = %.2f", p_nash),
           hjust = 1, size = 3.4, color = "steelblue") +
  annotate("text", x = p_H + 0.015, y = 0.45,
           label = sprintf("herd immunity\np[H] = %.2f", p_H),
           hjust = 0, size = 3.4, color = "firebrick") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.03, y = r + 0.035,
           label = "relative vaccine cost r", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.4, color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Vaccination coverage p",
       y = expression("Infection risk if unvaccinated, " * pi(p))) +
  theme_minimal()

One identity worth noticing: at an interior equilibrium, everyone’s expected cost is exactly — vaccinators pay by construction, and non-vaccinators face risk . This will make welfare comparisons easy below.

4 Two coupled populations

Now the setting the title promised. Two populations of equal size (label them 1 and 2), coupled by a next-generation matrix

where is within-population transmission and is between-population transmission. Each population independently arrives at its own voluntary coverage . The final sizes among the unvaccinated now solve a coupled system:

The strategic structure is the same as before, applied within each population: coverage in population adjusts until (or hits a boundary). But now depends on , and vice versa — which is exactly the condition for the game between populations to have interesting equilibria.

# Coupled final sizes among the unvaccinated, by fixed-point iteration
attack_rates2 <- function(p, K, tol = 1e-12, max_iter = 5000) {
  z <- c(1, 1)
  for (i in seq_len(max_iter)) {
    z_new <- 1 - exp(-as.vector(K %*% ((1 - p) * z)))
    if (max(abs(z_new - z)) < tol) break
    z <- z_new
  }
  z
}

# Population i's equilibrium coverage, given the other population's coverage:
# raise p_i until the local infection risk falls to r (with boundary cases)
best_response <- function(p_other, i, K, r) {
  f <- function(p_i) {
    p <- numeric(2); p[i] <- p_i; p[-i] <- p_other
    attack_rates2(p, K)[i] - r
  }
  if (f(0) <= 0) return(0)   # risk already below cost: no one vaccinates
  if (f(1) >= 0) return(1)   # spillover risk exceeds cost even at full coverage
  uniroot(f, c(0, 1), tol = 1e-9)$root
}

# 90% of contacts within, 10% between; rows sum to R0 = 2.5
K <- matrix(c(2.25, 0.25,
              0.25, 2.25), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

A Nash equilibrium of the two-population game is a pair where each coverage is a best response to the other. We can find it by iterating best responses until they stop moving:

p <- c(0.5, 0.5)
for (it in 1:200) {
  p_new <- c(best_response(p[2], 1, K, r),
             best_response(p[1], 2, K, r))
  if (max(abs(p_new - p)) < 1e-10) break
  p <- p_new
}
p_nash2 <- p
round(c(p1 = p_nash2[1], p2 = p_nash2[2],
        risk1 = attack_rates2(p_nash2, K)[1],
        risk2 = attack_rates2(p_nash2, K)[2]), 3)
   p1    p2 risk1 risk2 
0.554 0.554 0.200 0.200

The symmetric equilibrium is — numerically identical to the single-population Nash coverage. That is not a coincidence: on the diagonal , the coupling is invisible, because an individual’s total exposure depends only on the row sum . The coupling shows its teeth off the diagonal, in the shape of the best-response curves.

grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
br1 <- sapply(grid, best_response, i = 1, K = K, r = r)  # p1 responding to p2
br2 <- sapply(grid, best_response, i = 2, K = K, r = r)  # p2 responding to p1

p_opt <- c(0.6, 0.6)  # social optimum, computed in the next section

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = br1, y = grid, color = "Population 1's best response"),
            linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_line(aes(x = grid, y = br2, color = "Population 2's best response"),
            linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey70") +
  annotate("point", x = p_nash2[1], y = p_nash2[2], size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = p_nash2[1] + 0.03, y = p_nash2[2] - 0.045,
           label = "Nash equilibrium\n(0.55, 0.55)", hjust = 0, size = 3.4) +
  annotate("point", x = p_opt[1], y = p_opt[2], shape = 18, size = 4.5,
           color = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = p_opt[1] + 0.03, y = p_opt[2] + 0.045,
           label = "social optimum\n(0.60, 0.60)", hjust = 0, size = 3.4,
           color = "grey30") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Population 1's best response" = "steelblue",
                                "Population 2's best response" = "firebrick"),
                     name = NULL) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = expression("Coverage in population 1, " * p[1]),
       y = expression("Coverage in population 2, " * p[2])) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Both curves slope downward: coverages are strategic substitutes. Read population 1’s curve (blue) at two points:

round(c(br1_when_p2_is_0.3 = best_response(0.3, 1, K, r),
        br1_when_p2_is_0.9 = best_response(0.9, 1, K, r)), 3)
br1_when_p2_is_0.3 br1_when_p2_is_0.9 
             0.753              0.506

If population 2 is stuck at 30% coverage — supply constraints, hesitancy, a later campaign start — population 1’s voluntary equilibrium rises to 75%, compensating for the imported risk. If population 2 reaches 90%, population 1 relaxes to 51%, free-riding on its neighbor’s effort. Every unit of coverage a neighbor adds is partly absorbed as reduced effort at home. This is the two-population echo of the 2×2 game above: the same incentive that produced the (C, N) equilibrium now bends a whole curve.

4.1 The social optimum, and the price of anarchy

A benevolent planner controlling both populations would minimize total per-capita cost — vaccination costs plus infection costs:

total_cost <- function(p, K, r) {
  z <- attack_rates2(p, K)
  mean(r * p + (1 - p) * z)
}

grid_opt <- expand.grid(p1 = seq(0, 1, by = 0.005),
                        p2 = seq(0, 1, by = 0.005))
cost <- mapply(function(a, b) total_cost(c(a, b), K, r),
               grid_opt$p1, grid_opt$p2)
opt <- grid_opt[which.min(cost), ]

round(c(p1_opt = opt$p1, p2_opt = opt$p2,
        cost_optimum = min(cost),
        cost_nash = total_cost(p_nash2, K, r)), 3)
      p1_opt       p2_opt cost_optimum    cost_nash 
        0.60         0.60         0.12         0.20

The planner pushes both populations to the herd-immunity threshold and eliminates the epidemic, at a per-capita cost of . The Nash equilibrium costs per capita — recall the identity from the single-population game: at an interior equilibrium, everyone’s expected cost equals exactly. The ratio, about 1.7, is the price of anarchy: society pays two-thirds more under decentralized decisions than under coordination, and it pays it in infections rather than in vaccine doses.

Note what the planner’s solution requires: both populations exceed their Nash coverage simultaneously. If only one moves to 0.6 while the other best-responds, the other slides down its curve, and the pair drifts back toward the equilibrium. That is precisely why the Nash equilibrium is the right baseline for policy analysis — it is where the system returns when coordination fails. Klepac and colleagues develop this logic for real cross-border vaccination decisions, asking when regional agreements are self-enforcing, meaning that the agreed coverage is itself a Nash equilibrium of the game between countries (4).

5 Reading Klepac et al. (2011)

A natural next read is Klepac, Laxminarayan and Grenfell’s synthesis of epidemiological and economic optima for a two-patch system (5). Their Figure 2 is built exactly like our Figure 2: the black lines are best-response curves (“cost minimizing coverage values at one patch for a given coverage in the other patch”), the black circle is their intersection — the Nash equilibrium — and the blue circle is the global optimum. Everything above transfers directly to reading that figure. Three ingredients differ, though, and they matter for interpreting the results.

1. The players are patch-level planners, not individuals. In our game so far, individuals within each population vaccinate until their personal risk equals their personal cost, . In Klepac et al., the player is the patch — a health ministry choosing to minimize its total local cost, vaccination plus infection, given the neighbor’s coverage. This is a different best response: a planner internalizes the herd protection that each dose confers on its own unvaccinated residents, which an individual decision-maker ignores. We can compute it with the same machinery by replacing the indifference condition with a cost minimization:

# Patch i's total per-capita cost, given its own and the neighbor's coverage
local_cost <- function(p_i, p_other, i, K, r) {
  p <- numeric(2); p[i] <- p_i; p[-i] <- p_other
  r * p_i + (1 - p_i) * attack_rates2(p, K)[i]
}

# Planner best response: minimize local cost (grid search — the cost surface
# has a kink at the elimination boundary, so avoid smooth optimizers)
planner_br <- function(p_other, i, K, r, grid = seq(0, 1, by = 0.0025)) {
  costs <- vapply(grid, local_cost, numeric(1),
                  p_other = p_other, i = i, K = K, r = r)
  grid[which.min(costs)]
}

# Is the social optimum (0.6, 0.6) a Nash equilibrium of the planner game?
round(c(br_to_0.6 = planner_br(0.6, 1, K, r),
        cost_at_0.60 = local_cost(0.60, 0.6, 1, K, r),
        cost_at_0.55 = local_cost(0.55, 0.6, 1, K, r),
        cost_at_0.65 = local_cost(0.65, 0.6, 1, K, r)), 3)
   br_to_0.6 cost_at_0.60 cost_at_0.55 cost_at_0.65 
       0.600        0.120        0.178        0.130

The planner’s best response to a neighbor at 0.6 is exactly 0.6, and unilateral deviations in either direction raise local costs. So for our symmetric patches, — the global optimum — is a Nash equilibrium of the planner game. This is the first thing to know when reading the paper: with patch planners as players, Klepac et al. find that for symmetric or weakly coupled patches “local optimal strategies agree with the global cost-effective strategy.” The tragedy of the individual-level game largely disappears, because each planner already internalizes the within-patch externality; what remains is only the (smaller) cross-border externality. Their interesting divergences — Nash and global optimum splitting apart — require strong coupling combined with asymmetries, for example one patch with an expensive delivery system, which is the configuration of their Figure 2B.

p2_grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.02)
br_ind <- sapply(p2_grid, best_response, i = 1, K = K, r = r)
br_pln <- sapply(p2_grid, planner_br, i = 1, K = K, r = r)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(p2_grid, br_ind, color = "Individuals (risk = cost)"),
            linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_line(aes(p2_grid, br_pln, color = "Local planner (min. local cost)"),
            linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey70") +
  annotate("point", x = p_nash2[1], y = p_nash2[1], size = 3,
           color = "steelblue") +
  annotate("text", x = p_nash2[1] + 0.03, y = p_nash2[1] - 0.09,
           label = "individual Nash (0.55)", hjust = 0, size = 3.4,
           color = "steelblue") +
  annotate("point", x = 0.6, y = 0.6, size = 3, color = "firebrick") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6 + 0.03, y = 0.6 + 0.09,
           label = "planner Nash =\nsocial optimum (0.60)", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.4, color = "firebrick") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Individuals (risk = cost)" = "steelblue",
                                "Local planner (min. local cost)" = "firebrick"),
                     name = NULL) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = expression("Neighbor's coverage, " * p[2]),
       y = expression("Population 1's best response, " * p[1])) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

2. Endemic equilibrium, not final size. Their epidemiological engine is an SIR model with births and deaths and a constant trickle of imported infections; costs are evaluated at the endemic equilibrium prevalence , rather than over a one-shot epidemic as here. The strategic analysis is unchanged — only the payoff function feeding the best responses is different. One practical consequence: the immigration term keeps prevalence strictly positive below the threshold, which smooths away the knife-edge elimination boundary of the final-size model. (In our model, that knife edge is why the asymmetric strong-coupling case is best explored with their machinery rather than ours: with a hard frontier, a whole segment of the frontier can consist of equilibria.)

3. Convex campaign costs — and an optimum independent of transmission. Their vaccination cost is exponential in coverage, , reflecting the rising marginal cost of reaching the last unvaccinated child. Combined with vaccination at birth and linear infection costs, this yields their most striking single-population result: the economic optimum does not depend on the transmission rate at all. The reason is visible in the endemic-prevalence formula: since , the marginal reduction in per unit of coverage is — a constant. Each additional dose buys the same reduction in prevalence whatever the pathogen’s transmissibility, so the optimum is set entirely by the ratio of disease burden to campaign costs. Our constant per-dose cost cannot reproduce this; if you extend the code above, the cost function is the first thing to upgrade.

With those three translations in hand, the paper’s headline findings read as extensions of Figure 2 and Figure 3: weak coupling or symmetry planner Nash global optimum (their Fig. 2A); strong coupling plus cost asymmetries the optima diverge and local incentives can preclude elimination that would be globally optimal (their Fig. 2B); and under budget constraints, the long-term global optimum can even direct one patch’s resources into its neighbor’s campaign (their Fig. 3) — herd immunity purchased where it is cheapest.

6 Practical takeaway

For a modeler who wants to use this on actual multi-population vaccination questions:

  1. Treat coverage as an equilibrium, not a knob. When uptake is voluntary, the coverage your compartmental model should expect is the solution of , not the target written in the strategy document. The indifference condition converts your existing final-size or transmission machinery directly into a behavioral prediction.
  2. Best-response curves are cheap to compute and very informative. Everything in this post ran on base R plus uniroot and a fixed-point loop. The slope of the curves tells you the direction of the externality: downward-sloping curves mean neighbor effort substitutes for local effort, so a donor-funded campaign in one district partially displaces voluntary uptake next door — an effect worth building into campaign impact estimates.
  3. The gap between Nash and optimum is the case for coordination. The price of anarchy quantifies, in the same cost units as a cost-effectiveness analysis, what regional coordination mechanisms (pooled procurement, synchronized campaigns, cross-border agreements) are worth. And an agreement will only hold if no signatory gains by unilaterally cutting coverage — that is, if the agreement is itself a Nash equilibrium (4).

The model here is deliberately minimal — equal population sizes, a perfect vaccine, symmetric costs, one-shot decisions. Each relaxation (asymmetric sizes, waning, sequential campaigns, more than two populations) changes the numbers but not the method: write down each player’s cost, compute best responses, and find where they intersect.

7 References
